newsitem.title: USA: U.S. high court weighs Ohio tax on gas marketers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. high court weighs Ohio tax on gas marketers.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday weighed whether the State of Ohio had violated the Constitution by imposing a natural gas use tax on product sold by marketers but not on product sold by local utilities.

The case involved a challenge by General Motors Corp to Ohio's 62-year old law exempting natural gas sold by utilities from a sales and use tax. The company argued that the law discriminated against sales by marketers, including out-of-state marketers, and impeded interstate trade.
Justices probed GM's argument, rejected by state courts, that Ohio should treat utilities and marketers equally.
"It seems to me that your theory would really eviscerate the regulation of public utilities," said Justice Sandra Day O'Connor, addressing GM's attorney, Timothy Dyk of Jones, Day, Reavis and Pogue.

Dyk replied that public utility regulation was not the issue, because Ohio's utilities were allowed to sell gas in the unregulated market, competing directly against marketers. Therefore, the exemption for utilities from the five to seven percent sales and use tax was unfair.
"Don't you have to look at their entire business, not just the part you single out?" asked Chief Justice Rehnquist.

His question was in line with the state's argument that utilities should be treated differently because, unlike marketers, they had a duty to provide service to all homes and had to pay a gross receipts tax.
"Marketers are trying to reach over this regulatory wall and pick off some of the benefits without sharing in the burdens," State Solicitor Jeffrey Sutton said.

The state also argued that there was no evidence that public utility sales during the contested period, 1987 through 1989, had been unregulated. "Every single sale in question was a tariff sale," said Sutton.
But Dyk said it should not matter whether any volume of the utilities' sales were in the regulated or unregulated market.
"Where you have a competitive gas market, you cannot favor in-state interests just because it has public utility status," he said.

Natural gas producers and marketers are closely watching the case out out of concern that if Ohio is allowed to treat utilities and marketers differently, other states might do the same, giving utilities a leg up in selling natural gas to industrial customers.
